A.explanation: With $m \approx 1000 \text{ kg}$ and $v \approx 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \approx 5 \times 10^4 \text{ J}$, a sensible town-driving value.

B.explanation: About 1000 times too large, it would need a speed near $300 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ for a $1000 \text{ kg}$ car.

C.explanation: About a million times too large, far beyond chemical fuel energy available to a small car in town.

D.explanation: About a billion times too large, comparable to very large-scale energy releases, not a town car.

hints: Notice the wording - a small car in a town - so estimate a mass near $1000 \text{ kg}$ and a town speed near $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Connect those estimates to kinetic energy with $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ where $v$ is squared, so speed matters most.
Calculate $0.5 \times 1000 \times 10^2$ in $\text{J}$ and check which power of ten, $10^4$ or $10^7$ or larger, it is closest to.
walkthrough: Identify what to estimate: mass of a small car is about $m \approx 1000 \text{ kg}$ and town speed is about $v \approx 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the governing rule for translational kinetic energy: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Substitute the estimates with units: $E_k \approx 0.5 \times 1000 \text{ kg} \times (10 \text{ m s}^{-1})^2$.
Do the intermediate calculation: $(10 \text{ m s}^{-1})^2 = 100 \text{ m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}$, so $E_k \approx 0.5 \times 1000 \times 100 = 5 \times 10^4 \text{ J}$.
Check order of magnitude: even $15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives about $1 \times 10^5 \text{ J}$, still closest to $10^4$-$10^5 \text{ J}$ and far from $10^7 \text{ J}$.
Therefore the reasonable estimate is $5 \times 10^4 \text{ J}$. This is option A.
